The Effect of Early Initiation of Physiotherapy on the
Functional Recovery of Dogs That Underwent Femoral
Head Ostectomy
Vahid Khazayee
Ehsan Emamjomeh
Mohamadreza Paryani
Department of Basic Science, Faculty of Veterinary Medicine, Karaj Branch, Islamic Azad University, Karaj, Iran
Correspondence: Mohamadreza Paryani (mrparyani@yahoo.com)
Received: 12 April 2024
Revised: 7 December 2024
Accepted: 17 January 2025
Funding: The authors received no specific funding for this work.
Keywords: physiotherapy | rehabilitation | surgery
ABSTRACT
Background: Some hip or femur disorders lead to femoral head osteotomy surgery. After surgery, it is necessary to start physical
therapy for faster recovery of the animal. Physiotherapy includes different devices such as stimulators or lasers and methods like
manual therapy and massage.
Objectives: This study was conducted to show the different methods of physiotherapy used in 19 dogs after femoral head
osteotomy, and also to collect information about the time between the start of physiotherapy after surgery and the duration of
their recovery.
Method: Nineteen dogs that underwent femoral head osteotomy surgery were given physiotherapy after 2 days. The treatment
methods used are cold therapy and heat therapy, ultrasound, laser therapy, electrical stimulation, massage, passive joint movement
and passive stretching. Lameness score and muscle size were measured at the beginning of physiotherapy and at the tenth session.
Result: There was no significant difference between the size of the muscles at the beginning of the physiotherapy session and the
10 sessions after that, but the evaluation of the lameness score showed a significant difference.
Conclusion: Early start of physiotherapy after surgery is very important and leads to faster recovery of the patient.
1
Introduction
Strong ligaments, joint capsules and muscles sustain a canine hip
joint in a normal state. Hip dysplasia or osteoarthritis has differ-
ent degrees of synovitis, articular cartilage eburnation, osteophyte
formation, sub-chondral bone sclerosis and remodelling among
the confirmed abnormalities in the hip joint and supporting
tissue (Barr et al. 1987). Fifty per cent of dogs suffer from muscle
atrophy after femoral head ostectomy (FHO) surgery (Engstig
et al. 2022). A typical operation on the coxofemoral joint is femoral
head and neck osteotomy surgery, which aims to lessen bone
contact between the femoral head and acetabulum and promote
the development of a pseudoarthrosis, or fake joint, made of
dense fibrous tissue. Aseptic necrosis of the femoral head (Legg–
Calvé–Perthes disease), joint laxity, hip luxation, osteoarthritis,
hip bone fractures, hip dysplasia and problems from total hip
replacement surgery are among the conditions that may warrant
consideration for an FHO operation (Reddy et al. 2024). With
an increase in the dog’s body weight, the hip joint’s articulating
surface’s exposed nerve endings and inflammatory alterations
create pain while the dog is moving. The size of the dog, the
timing of the surgical intervention and the utilization of physical
therapy within 48 h of an orthopaedic surgical operation all play
a role in the procedure’s success to some extent (Chaudhary et al.

2020). Dogs frequently undergo FHO as a form of salvage surgery.
Coxofemoral luxations, traumatic femoral head/neck fractures,
acetabular fractures, aseptic femoral head necrosis and end-stage
coxofemoral osteoarthritis are all indications of FHO. Sciatic
nerve injury and iatrogenic femoral fracture are perioperative
FHO consequences (Off and Matis 2010).
Physiotherapy is a rapidly expanding area of medical science
that was initially connected to neurology and orthopaedics. A
distinct physiotherapist profession emerged as a result of the
gradual development of rehabilitation techniques and assistance
for the treatment of musculoskeletal disorders and neuropathies.
A physiotherapist’s duties include evaluating the patient’s motor

dysfunctions and developing and implementing effective treat-
ment strategies (Dybczyńska et al. 2022). Animal physiotherapy
is currently successfully employed in agricultural animals as
well as, in rare circumstances, in wild, live animal species, such
as those held in zoos. It is no longer limited to companion
animals. Patients of all ages both humans and animals can receive
physiotherapy based on protocols that are individualized for their
needs (Griffiths 2014).
The goal of this research is to develop a targeted and effective
treatment plan for patients who had FHO surgery by utilizing
standard therapeutic techniques and associated equipment, so
the current retrospective study was carried out.
2
Method
Nineteen dogs were enlisted for this study and underwent
physiotherapy employing a diverse array of techniques. Among
these canines, 11 were female, while the remainder were male.
Their ages spanned from 1 to 6 years, with weights ranging
from 1.3 to 12.8 kg. All participants were of purebred lineage,
except for one of mixed breed. Various conditions, such as hip
dysplasia, acetabulum fracture, hip luxation, aseptic necrosis
femoral head and head femoral fracture, necessitated FHO
procedures in these dogs. Clinical signs in dogs included a
lameness score between 2 and 5 along with pain. Patient clinical
records encompassed details regarding age, gender, breed, weight,
thigh circumference, count of physiotherapy sessions and limb
functional recovery (Table 1). Thigh circumference (Table 2),
with hair left untrimmed, was measured twice or thrice at 50%
of thigh length using the same measuring tape (Baker et al.
2010). Leash walking was recommended to owners (Millis and
Levine 2013). The initial measurement took place prior to the
first physiotherapy session, the second after 10 sessions and
the third upon the dog’s attainment of unhindered mobility,
except for one dog exhibiting residual lameness. Before each
physiotherapy session, a history was taken from the owners to
check all types of accidents such as injuries or possible wounds
to ensure the absence of other causes of lameness. In addition,
movement organs were examined to observe possible wounds
caused by walking. Also, a radiology study was done before
surgery and 1 month after surgery (Figure 1). Physiotherapy
sessions were categorized into groups: 1–10, 11–20 and exceeding
20 sessions (Colvero et al. 2020). Lameness was assessed by
following instructions: No visual lameness (Grade 0), mild lame-
ness with minimal head/pelvic movement (Grade 1), moderate
lameness with normal step length and partial weight bearing
(Grade 2) and reduced step length. Moderate lameness with
partial weight-bearing (Grade 3), severe lameness with minimal
use of the limbs (Grade 4) and non–weight-bearing lameness
(Grade 5) (Brønniche Møller Nielsen et al. 2020). The pain
score before and after surgery was not measured because the
animal’s behaviour was different in the clinic and at home. Each
modality of physical therapy adhered to established literature
recommendations, encompassing neuromuscular electrical stim-
ulation (NMES) (Pelizzari et al. 2008), superficial thermotherapy
(hot water shower) (Dorn 2015), therapeutic ultrasound (US) in
continuous mode with 3 MHz frequency and intensities ranging
from 0.3 to 1 W/cm2 (Hanks et al. 2015), high power laser (Millis
and Levine 2013), passive joint movement (MPA) (Marcellin-
Little and Levine 2015), passive stretching (PS) and massage (M)
(Colvero et al. 2020). Since they were all neutered, they were
fed Royal Canine sterilized food. Statistical analysis employed
the SPSS software, utilizing the Mann–Whitney test to ascertain
correlations between session count and functional recovery, also
this test examined correlations with muscle mass size.
3
Results
The table presents separate data for the lameness scores and
muscle sizes of the samples. According to the results of the Mann–
Whitney test, there was a significant improvement in lameness
scores (Figure 2) after 10 sessions of the prescribed therapy
(***p < 0.0001). However, the change in muscle size (Figure 3)
did not reach statistical significance (p = 0.5391).
4
Discussion
This study is grounded entirely in contemporary and prominent
veterinary physiotherapy sources, striving to incorporate modern
devices and methodologies whenever feasible. Adherence to
established guidelines for each method’s application, tailored

to specific surgical techniques and operation durations, was a
priority. The objective of this study was to contribute novel
insights to the field of veterinary physiotherapy at both national
and international levels.
FHO surgery is undertaken for various reasons, including hip
dysplasia, femoral neck fracture, hip fracture, epiphyseal or
femoral neck fracture and aseptic/vascular necrosis of the femoral
neck or head (Sabiza et al. 2019). Complications of FHO surgery
may include patellar dislocation (due to upper limb posterior
instability), muscle atrophy, reduced range of motion and lame-
ness, all of which can be addressed through timely physical
therapy (Jahandideh and Tabary 2020; Sabiza et al. 2019).
According to the findings of this study, prompt physical ther-
apy utilizing the mentioned methods in FHO dogs markedly
improved lameness scores. Additionally, early intervention min-
imized muscle atrophy, rendering the muscle size difference
variable statistically insignificant. The study supports initiating
physical therapy approximately 2 days post-surgery (Dycus et al.
2017).

full rehabilitation within 10 sessions and showed no signs of
lameness, and the muscles of the operated limb; they were
close to the size of healthy body muscles. Conversely, Colvero
et al. 2020) rejected correlation and showed no detectable
relationship between initiation of physical therapy and patient
recovery.
The authors suggest that the majority of patients required
approximately 10 sessions of physiotherapy, with only 4 patients
necessitating more than 20 sessions, largely due to the timely
initiation of sessions. Fibrous tissue formation around the joint,
if delayed, can lead to pain and restricted movement, potentially
resulting in muscle atrophy and delayed recovery (Baltzer 2020).
In this study, all patients commenced physiotherapy sessions
2 days post-surgery, resulting in approximately 63% returning
to normal within 28 days without lameness. Only around 21%
required more than 20 sessions and one patient experienced
persistent lameness until the continuation of physiotherapy
sessions. Considering a regimen of three sessions per week, 95% of
patients achieved complete recovery within 63 days, underscoring
the importance of post-surgical physiotherapy. In a study by
Barbosa, FHO surgery patients attained complete recovery after
1296 days, emphasizing the pivotal role of physiotherapy in
expediting patient recovery (Barbosa et al. 2012).
In the Colvero study, which examined 20 dogs undergoing FHO
surgery, it was observed that patients required longer treatment
and exhibited slower recovery compared to the findings of this
study. This discrepancy may be attributed to delayed initiation
of physical therapy. Only four patients commenced treatment
on the fifth day post-surgery, and even among them, those
whose physiotherapy began 2 months after surgery experienced
complete recovery. Additionally, the broader array of sports
and physiotherapy techniques utilized in their study yielded
delayed treatment responses. These findings underscore the
critical importance of initiating physical therapy promptly for
optimal outcomes (Colvero et al. 2020).
Furthermore, the use of cold therapy within the initial 72 h post-
surgery significantly reduced inflammation and pain, thereby
shortening the patients’ rehabilitation period (Millis and Ciu-
perca 2015). While conventional wisdom suggests performing
cold therapy 3–5 days after surgery (Steiss and Levine 2005), the
authors contend that better outcomes can be achieved if this
intervention is administered within the first 3 days post-surgery.
Thermotherapy, comprising continuous therapeutic US and hot
water showers, was employed to induce local warming and
enhance tissue extensibility and blood circulation, thus alleviat-
ing pain and facilitating stretching, MPA and joint amplitude gain
(Baltzer 2020; Davidson et al. 2005; Hanks et al. 2015; Millis and
Ciuperca 2015).
Subsequent to ultrasound or hot water shower sessions, all
animals received M, PS and MPA. M was recommended to
alleviate muscle tension by interrupting the spasm–painspasm
cycle (Millis and Levine 2013; Sharp 2012) and priming the
muscles for exercise (Drum et al. 2015). PS and MPA were
prescribed to enhance joint flexibility, periarticular tissue extensi-
bility and muscle elasticity (Souza et al. 2006), thereby improving
range of motion and contributing to joint health maintenance

(Marcellin-Little and Levine 2015).
NMES, particularly Russian stimulation, encourages muscle con-
traction, mitigates disuse-induced atrophy and muscle strength
loss and promotes tissue healing by enhancing blood supply
5 of 7
(Doyle 2004; Evans et al. 2013). For these reasons, electrical
stimulation was used in all sessions.
In equine studies, high-dose laser therapy improved lame-
ness scores, attributed to its anti-inflammatory and analgesic
effects on tendons and ligaments. Laser therapy transforms
prostaglandins into prostacyclin, mitigating inflammation and
suppresses nociceptors, providing pain relief. Additionally,
laser light induces hyperaemia and microvascularization, fos-
tering an anti-oedema effect (Zielińska et al. 2020). Laser
therapy also contributes to early bone repair, increased col-
lagen deposition and bone trabeculae, adjunct treatment of
osteomyelitis, fibrous healing of cartilaginous defects and main-
tenance of cartilage in immobilized joints (Millis and Levine
2013).
According to studies, unlike veterinary medicine, in humans,
the rehabilitation caused by periacetabular osteotomy surgery
is based on exercise therapy and active or passive range of
motion, with the difference that the PROM occurs earlier in
animals (Disantis et al. 2022). Also, after total hip replacement
surgery, most studies recommend the use of exercise therapy,
and few studies were found by researchers who used physical
therapy devices such as laser or electrical stimulation. However,
all studies indicated the potential impact of rehabilitation after
surgery and showed that after 1 year, the difference in quality
of life between those who underwent rehabilitation and those
who were not was significant (Costa et al. 2021). Based on
these data, the authors suggest that a study be conducted on
dogs whose rehabilitation programme is only based on exercise
therapy.
In this study, we tried to use the most up-to-date and reliable
methods. Although measuring with a tape has been confirmed
by studies, but due to the lack of a suitable probe size for the
ultrasound machine, it would be better to check the size of
the muscles by ultrasound. On the other hand, measuring the
range of motion and the angle of the joints are very important
diagnostic factors in evaluating the recovery of patients, but due
to the aggressiveness of some cases or severe muscle contraction
due to fear and anxiety, no accurate data were obtained. It
is suggested to use these methods for evaluation in future
studies.
5
Conclusion
FHO surgery can lead to numerous post-operative complications.
Initiating physical therapy promptly has been shown to expedite
rehabilitation in dogs and mitigate the extent of atrophy resulting
from surgery. For future research endeavours, it is advisable
to employ a singular physiotherapy method, allowing for a
focused examination of each rehabilitation modality’s mecha-
nism of action. Moreover, increasing the sample size would
enhance the robustness of the findings. Given that variables
such as age, gender, weight and breed were not standardized
in this study, it is recommended that researchers address these
factors to ensure the reliability of the results in subsequent
studies. Standardizing these parameters will facilitate a more
accurate comparison of outcomes across different interventions
and patient demographics.
